title: Stop Adding & Start Improving
author: The Disruptive Educator
source: The Disruptive Educator on Substack, December 8, 2025
summary: The premise flips the usual PL complaint on its head. The author has watched schools run 'checking for understanding' sessions every year for six years, and concedes the optics: doesn't that look obsessive? No, they argue. Expertise does not exempt a teacher from learning; it heightens the responsibility to keep refining. Sitting in another colleague's session on a topic you teach and research yourself is not redundancy, it is where the next iteration surfaces. Novelty is not the point. Return is. The middle of the piece names the structural problem. Schools treat PL like a menu: taste the topic of the term, move on, brand a new focus for the next cycle. The research on implementation says moving from exploration to fidelity on a single technique takes years, not weeks. Despite that, initiatives are routinely abandoned after a term, driven by what the author calls leadership impatience and novelty addiction. The visible result is the cycle Tim will recognise: teachers nod politely, attend the session, invest minimally, because history has taught them that good ideas do not stay long enough to matter. The corrective is not more exposure but better conditions. Time, coaching, feedback, repetition, and accountability applied to fewer techniques over longer horizons. Leaders have to give staff permission to return to the same concept until it's good, then again until it's better. Teachers carry a parallel responsibility: accept that you can be brilliant at a technique and still have room to sharpen it, and shift from 'we've already done this' to 'how are we improving it.' The most effective teams the author has worked with are cultures where staff are both confident and unfinished.
points: The central argument of this piece is grounded in the author's engagement with how real people think and act, not in idealized or abstract reasoning.
The takeaway is actionable,it can be implemented at the classroom or school level without waiting for policy change or external resources.
The piece challenges a common default assumption in education practice and offers a concrete alternative framed by evidence or lived experience.
The stakes are clear: what happens if leaders or teachers adopt this approach, and what is the cost of continuing the current default.
quotes: I took a genuine interest in the research behind it, which led me to publicly present on checks for understanding in early 2023, and it is woven through my current research studies. Even this year, at researchED Ballarat, I presented on responsive maths teaching (essentially checks for understanding in a mathematics context) and sat in Bron Ryrie-Jones’ brilliant session on the very same topic on the same day.

From the outside, that might look a little obsessive. It might seem unusual to sit in on a session about something you teach and research yourself. But that is precisely the point. I walked away from Bron’s session with pages of notes, fresh ways of thinking and ideas I had not considered. Expertise does not exempt us from learning. If anything, it increases our responsibility to keep refining.

Schools often treat professional learning just like a menu though. We choose the topic of the term, taste it briefly and then move onto a new topic with good marketing. The problem is, even for topics that do yield greater progress for students or are effective in achieving their aims, expertise doesn’t sufficiently development from tasting.

Often teacher resistance is seen as being one of the biggest barriers to school change, but I’d posit that leadership impatience is a far bigger barrier. Schools are often so eager to demonstrate momentum with new initiatives, complete with flashy social media marketing, that they equate exposure with progress.

It isn’t uncommon for schools to abandon an initiative after a term to either move onto the next popular thing or because somehow 2 months wasn’t enough time to totally transform results. The only result of this is initiative fatigue for staff. Teachers aren’t given the opportunity to become experts because they are rarely given the time or support to refine their work to the point of mastery.

School improvement can certainly be a knowledge problem, but it’s also a conditions problem. Rather than exposure to more ideas, staff need time to move a little deeper than surface level on the existing ideas that evidence tells us works. This means time, feedback, repetition and accountability to refine the techniques that matter.

Teachers aren’t afraid of improvement. We’re exhausted by shiny popular instructional techniques that continually reappear with a new name like a trend that just won’t die. The truth of it is though that you can be a brilliant teacher and be brilliant at implementing a technique, but still have room to sharpen it.

Schools that make real impact aren’t about chasing novelty. They double down on what works and refuse to move until it has teeth. Their staff review the same principles time and time again with a focus on doing them better. They choose fewer ideas, but chase them faster.” Archived from The Disruptive Educator on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
